source.title: Scaling laws for language encoding models in fMRI
source.authors: Richard J. Antonello; Aditya R. Vaidya; Alexander G. Huth

record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling analyses to a new setting—fMRI brain-response encoding—and reports how downstream encoding performance varies with model size. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes are fMRI encoding performance, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy or training compute. Model-size results bear on V6 only. The OPT-125M and Whisper Large fMRI training-data-size results concern the size of the brain dataset, not language-model pretraining tokens; they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study asks whether scaling 'laws' hold for a new downstream task, predicting fMRI brain responses. It measures how encoding performance changes with OPT and Whisper model size, which bears on V6. Pretraining loss is never fitted against scale, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that encoding performance scales logarithmically with LM size up to ~30B (~15% gain) and with fMRI dataset size. Larger hidden states worsen regression conditioning with finite data, so OPT and LLaMA peak near 30B. Audio models show comparable scaling with no plateau yet. A noise-ceiling analysis shows some areas (precuneus, higher auditory cortex) near the maximum. They recommend larger models and deep datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits linear fMRI encoding models from neural-network representations and evaluates prediction of held-out brain responses; it does not fit language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling curves or optimize a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The parameter-scaling result depends on selecting the best-performing layer at each model size. OPT performance plateaus above approximately 30B in the finite-fMRI-data setting; the authors attribute this to hidden-state size and regression conditioning. The fMRI dataset-size sweeps use OPT-125M layer 9 and Whisper Large layer 30.

fits_no_version.finding: Encoding performance for OPT-125M and Whisper Large rises log-linearly with the number of fMRI training stories (+122% and +144% per order of magnitude).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain-encoding performance scales logarithmically with subject-specific fMRI training data.

record.problems: The evaluation uses fMRI data from 3 human subjects. The authors report a plateau for larger OPT models and explain that finite fMRI data and increasing hidden-state size can limit encoding regression. The reported logarithmic trends concern brain-encoding performance, not held-out language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were made for individual plotted checkpoint values where the text reports only aggregate family-level trends; the relevant parameter sweeps are summarized in r1, r2, and r4. Layer-wise performance plots and noise-ceiling analyses do not measure the versions tested here.

untested.parts: No pretraining-loss power-law fits against parameters, tokens or compute. Table 2 gives OPT podcast perplexity by size, but no fit is made.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Loss power laws in audio models are not measured; only downstream encoding is measured.
Standard downstream language benchmarks are untested. Encoding performance as a function of pretraining loss is not fitted, though perplexities are listed.
Fitted loss exponents and their dependence on setup are not studied.

missing.what: OPT podcast perplexity by size: 125M 35.91, 1.3B 22.48, 13B 18.17, 30B 17.35, 66B 16.56. LLaMA 33B/66B: 10.21/9.73. Perplexity keeps falling past 30B while encoding plateaus, which bears on V6 via pretraining loss.
LLaMA 33B vs 66B encoding performance: peak near 30B, and LLaMA ~5% better than OPT, possibly due to more training tokens (1.4T vs 180B).
HuBERT (95M–964M) and WavLM (95M–317M) size scaling of encoding performance; the abstract reports comparable improvements with size.
In auditory cortex, Whisper encoding performance does not plateau with model size.

record.verdict_notes: Encoding performance is a downstream measure, and the fitted trend is logarithmic in parameters rather than a power law in loss. The plateau is tied to the encoding regression, not to the LMs themselves. Error bars are given only for the dataset-size sweeps. There are 3 subjects.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, pretraining tokens, or compute was not measured.
The study does not fit pretraining-loss curves on small runs and test predictions on larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between language-model parameters and pretraining tokens was evaluated.
The study does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count for language-model pretraining loss.
Audio models are used for brain encoding, but the study does not test whether language-model pretraining-loss power laws hold across modalities or training regimes.
Only fMRI brain-response encoding performance versus model parameter count is tested. Downstream language-task performance and its relation to pretraining loss are not tested.
The study does not test setup-dependent pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations. Its fMRI encoding-performance plateau is a different measure.

rows.value: Approximately logarithmic scaling; average-subject encoding performance increases roughly 4.4% per order-of-magnitude increase in parameters; r = 0.91

rows.check: It is ambiguous whether the r = 0.91 fit covers 125M–30B only or all six OPT sizes. The text says it covers the six sizes and then 'tapers off'. The abstract's ~15% overall gain over 125M–30B is a useful companion figure.

rows.measure: Average fMRI encoding performance versus parameter count
rows.value: The logarithmic relationship tapers off to a plateau for models in excess of approximately 30 billion parameters.
rows.note: The authors attribute the downturn at larger sizes to hidden-state dimensionality and limitations in the amount of fMRI training data.
rows.check: There is no further gain above ~30B. The Discussion says performance 'peaks at about 30B' and that wider models lower performance. That is no improvement beyond 30B, not a weaker one, so 'absent' fits better than 'partial'. The authors attribute it to ill-conditioned regression with finite fMRI data (33,000 points).
